title: Pagliacci
facts: Pagliacci premiered in Milan on 21 May 1892, conducted by Arturo Toscanini.
Critics were mixed at first, but the public loved Pagliacci instantly, and still does.
Leoncavallo, then little known, wrote Pagliacci after seeing the success of Mascagni’s Cavalleria rusticana.
Leoncavallo said the story came from his childhood: the 1865 murder of a family servant, a case his father, a judge, investigated.
The French author Catulle Mendès sued Leoncavallo for plagiarism; he later dropped the suit.
The Prologue was an afterthought: Leoncavallo wrote it to tempt the star baritone Victor Maurel into singing Tonio.
Baritones often add a high A-flat and G near the end of the Prologue, though they aren’t in the original score.
In Leoncavallo’s manuscript, Tonio (not Canio) sings the last line, “La commedia è finita!” Canio took it over around 1895.
In 1907 Pagliacci became the first opera recorded complete, under Leoncavallo’s personal supervision.
The Met first paired Pagliacci with Cavalleria rusticana in a double bill on 22 December 1893.
Jean de Reszke sang Canio at the 1902 Paris Opera premiere, his last public performance.
